# What a feeling wants {#what-a-feeling-wants}

## The gap {#gap}

An English emotion word such as *anxious*, *angry*, or *proud* names the feeling and says nothing more about it. *I'm so angry* does not say which need went unmet, or what the anger makes you want to do. *It made me anxious* can send you off to hide before you have noticed that hiding is what you want. Ageben names the need and the urge in one word, so you can name the urge before you follow it.

## The forms {#forms}
<!-- Agent summary: feeling word = thanks/sorry word (`th` + sake + `tha` met / `thu` unmet + ending) + urge vowel + last `-m`. Middle ending keeps its thanks/sorry meaning (how long the payoff or harm lasts); this lesson uses the default `-m`. Last `-m` = how long the feeling lasts, left open. Placement: after the English clause the feeling is about; alone, with no clause = a whole sentence about how you feel. Can't tell which sake → `uda` (`thudathumum`); naming the sake changes nothing else (`thunathumum`). Nothing makes you want to move → urge `a`. -->

A **feeling word** is one Ageben word that names a need and the **urge**, which is what the feeling makes you want to do. You build it from a thanks or sorry word from *Thanks and sorry*. That word starts with `th`, names a sake (the need involved), says with `tha` that the sake was met or with `thu` that it went unmet, and ends with an ending such as `-m`. To make a feeling word, keep that whole word, add one vowel for the urge, and end with another `-m`.

| `thuwa` | `tha` | `m` | `a` | `m` |
|---------|-------|-----|-----|-----|
| competence | met | default ending | stay in it (urge) | how long: open |

Read the table from left to right. `thuwatham` is the thanks word for competence met, *it worked; I can do this*. The urge `a` adds *I want to stay in it*, and the last `-m` ends the word, so `thuwathamam` says *I pulled it off, and I want to savor it*.

The ending from *Thanks and sorry*, which says how long the payoff or the harm lasts, now sits in the middle of the word and keeps that meaning. Every feeling word in this lesson keeps it at the default, `-m`. The last `-m` is about the feeling itself, and it leaves open how long the feeling lasts.

Put the feeling word after the English clause the feeling is about, as in *We shipped the draft `thuwathamam`*. A feeling word on its own, with no clause, is a whole sentence about how you feel.

When you can't tell which need is involved, use the unspecified sake `uda`. So `thudathumum` says *something is off, and I want to get away*. Once you can tell which need it is, put that sake in place of `uda` and change nothing else: `thunathumum` says *my say was taken, and I want to get away*. For the urge, when nothing makes you want to move, use `a`.

## The four urges {#urges}
<!-- Agent summary: urge vowel (table): `a` stay in it (*in*), `e` act on someone (*at*), `o` do something for someone (*for*), `u` move off (*from*). `a` points at no one; `e` `o` `u` move you relative to someone or something. *Belongs when* lists times each fits; no urge is the right one to have. Two urges mix → name the stronger one. -->

| Urge | It makes you want to | Belongs when |
|------|----------------------|--------------|
| `a` | stay in it: savor it, sit with it | it is a good moment, or a loss that needs time |
| `e` | act on someone: confront, thank, press for | something can be said or done to someone |
| `o` | do something for someone: give back, make amends | you were helped, or you caused a cost |
| `u` | move off: avoid, leave, hide | the danger is real, or you need room |

Each urge goes with one small English word that says which way the feeling moves you: `a` with *in*, `e` with *at*, `o` with *for*, and `u` with *from*. The words also sort the four into two groups. `a` means staying where you are, in the feeling, so it points at no one. The other three move you in relation to someone or something: `e` means acting at them, `o` doing something for them, and `u` moving away from them. So to pick the vowel, first ask whether the feeling makes you want to move at all, and if it does, which of those three ways.

The same event can bring different urges, and the vowel says which one you feel:

> My friend remembered my birthday `thawethamam`.  
> My friend remembered my birthday `thawethamem`.  
> I forgot to pick her up `thewathumom`.  
> I forgot to pick her up `thewathumum`.

Both birthday sentences say you feel connected. With `thawethamam` you want to stay in that feeling, and with `thawethamem` you want to act on someone, here by thanking your friend. Both of the last two say you cost her something. `thewathumom` says you want to make it right, and `thewathumum` says you want to get away, for example by avoiding her.

No urge is the right one to have. Each one fits some situations, and the *Belongs when* column names a few of them: wanting to move off fits when the danger is real. When two urges mix, as when you want both to thank your friend and to sit with the feeling, name the stronger one.

## Examples {#examples}

> We shipped the draft `thuwathamam`.  
> He rewrote my memo `thunathumem`.  
> I snapped at my sister `thewathumom`.  
> My friend called out of the blue `thawethamam`.  
> `thudathumum`, and I don't know why yet.

| Drop-in | What it says | Instead of | The parts |
|---------|--------------|------------|-----------|
| `thuwathamam` | *I pulled it off*, and I want to savor it | *proud* | competence met; stay in it |
| `thunathumem` | my say was taken, and I want to take it up with someone | *angry* | autonomy unmet; act on someone |
| `thewathumom` | I cost her something, and I want to make it right | *guilty* | beneficence unmet; do something for someone |
| `thawethamam` | I feel connected, and I want to stay in it | *touched* | relatedness met; stay in it |
| `thudathumum` | something is off, and I want to get away | *uneasy* | a sake unmet; move off |

`thunathumem` says you want to take it up with someone, and its sake says what you would ask for: a say in your own work. Where *guilty* names only the feeling, `thewathumom` names the cost: she is not better off because of you, and you want to make that right. `thudathumum` names an urge to get away before you know which need is behind it.

## Telling a feeling word apart {#telling-apart}
<!-- Agent summary: near misses. The urge is a want, not a decision: naming it leaves you free to follow it or not. Keep the English emotion word when it is all you can tell (no need, no urge). After a clause the feeling is about that clause's event; alone it is about nothing you can point to, and the clause can come later. -->

A feeling word is easily confused in three ways: its urge with a plan, the feeling word with the English emotion word, and the word after a clause with the same word alone.

### An urge or a plan {#urge-or-plan}

The urge is what the feeling makes you want to do, and naming it leaves you free to follow it or not. Compare these two:

> He rewrote my memo, and I'm going to talk to him.  
> He rewrote my memo `thunathumem`.

The first sentence says what you will do. The second says that your say was taken and that you want to take it up with someone. After saying it, you can still decide to let the memo go, because the word named a want and did not commit you to anything.

### A feeling word or the English word {#feeling-or-emotion-word}

*He rewrote my memo, and I'm angry* names the feeling. *He rewrote my memo `thunathumem`* names the need behind it and what the anger makes you want to do. So use the feeling word when you can tell those two things. When all you can tell is the emotion word, keep the English word, which says as much as you know.

### With a clause or alone {#clause-or-alone}

> The meeting ran two hours over `thudathumum`.  
> `thudathumum`.

After a clause, the feeling is about what the clause says happened, here the long meeting. On its own, the same word says that the feeling is about nothing you can point to. So you can say it before you know the cause, and add the clause once you find it.

## Practice {#practice}

Build the feeling word from the parts in the note.

**1.** *My friend remembered my favorite song.* (connection met, default ending; I want to stay in it)

::: details Show answer
My friend remembered my favorite song `thawethamam`.
:::

**2.** *My friend remembered my favorite song.* (connection met, default ending; I want to thank someone)

::: details Show answer
My friend remembered my favorite song `thawethamem`.
:::

**3.** *The meeting ran two hours over.* (my say went unmet, default ending; I want to take it up with someone)

::: details Show answer
The meeting ran two hours over `thunathumem`.
:::

**4.** *The meeting ran two hours over.* (my say went unmet, default ending; I want to get away)

::: details Show answer
The meeting ran two hours over `thunathumum`.
:::

**5.** How you feel right now, with no clause. (something is off, and I can't tell which need; I want to get away)

::: details Show answer
`thudathumum`.
:::
